newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela says new South Africa only beginning.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says new South Africa only beginning.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela could have used a stiff drink on Friday to get him through his first big speech of the year -- a cocktail of heady congratulations for the new South Africa mixed with sober warnings that it could all still end in tears.

"In a sense, this is the first session of the new parliament" since South Africa adopted a new constitution last year to bury the old apartheid regime, Mandela told the opening of parliament in Cape Town for its first session of 1997.

"Through the new constitution, we have laid the foundation for a peaceful and prosperous nation. But it is just that: a foundation. And it will not amount to much if its provisions are not felt in the daily life of our people," he said.
"The people come first, and our models, strategies and plans should be measured by this yardstick," Mandela said. But all South Africans should also realise they had duties as well as rights.

The speech came a day after armed clashes in a Johannesburg suburb exposed the explosive pressures in a society struggling to transform itself into a thriving democracy that is able to meet the expectations of all its 42 million people.

Mandela, credited with South Africa's "miracle transformation" to democratic rule in the 1990s from a tensely divided nation of white rulers and black have-nots, has served notice that he will make way soon for a younger leadership and quit public life in 1999.

Reviewing the accomplishments of the past year, and the mountain of tasks still to be completed, he warned that the new nation now being forged was burdened by daunting poverty, joblessness, crime, violence, corruption, and "terrible" public services.
The responsibilities facing his government were awesome, the 78-year-old head of state told a packed assembly.
Pausing to sip from a glass of water on the podium, Mandela made a face and joked: "I must confess I am disappointed. I thought they'd have given me something stronger."

Opposition leaders slated the speech as short on hard-edged specifics. But Mandela, whose address was televised live to the nation, appeared to be aiming more at ordinary South Africans than Cape Town legislators.

Often irked by media critics who fail to give his government the credit he feels it deserves, he extolled progress made in bringing food, water, electricity and health care to millions of people who were "neglected outcasts" under the former white-dominated government.

But government could not do everything, he said. There was a price to pay for success yet too many people appeared unwilling to do their share, and too many vital institutions were still locked in the slack practices of the past.

Unless there was a radical shakeup in the public service sector to eradicate corruption and inefficiency, "it will be difficult if not impossible to build on the foundation that has been laid", he said.
"We shall have good plans and even the resources to carry them out. But we shall year-in and year-out be saddled with unspent funds, terrible services and millions siphoned off in corrupt practices."

Mandela said the fight against violent crime which threatens to strangle South Africa's major cities, was hampered by a "ridiculously backward data base" which often allowed offenders to elude justice.
He pledged more strong medicine to turn back the crime wave, but again admonished citizens to look to their own responsibilities.

"When all is said and done, success depends on our whole society adopting a new value system," Mandela said. In buying stolen goods, evading tax and not paying for services "we become our worst enemies".
"We all want South Africa to succeed. But we must be prepared to foot the bill." he told the nation.
